question.en: What should a reliable CI/CD pipeline do from commit to production?

answer.en: A pipeline should build a reproducible artifact, run fast feedback checks such as linting and unit tests, run integration or acceptance validation, and promote the same artifact through controlled environments. It should stop on failed checks, record logs and artifacts, and make production promotion either automatically continuous or explicitly approved according to the delivery policy. Infrastructure changes should be part of the same reviewable process, not console-only steps. I also want post-deployment verification, observable health signals, and a defined rollback or forward-fix path. The important distinction is that continuous delivery keeps production promotion approvable, while continuous deployment removes that explicit approval gate.

question.en: A pipeline deploys every green build of main automatically to staging, but production requires a human approval. Is that continuous deployment?

answer.en: No, it is continuous delivery: every build is automated and production-ready, but promotion to production keeps an explicit approval gate. Continuous deployment removes that gate so a green build reaches production with no human decision. The distinguishing factor is the approval, not the amount of automation (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/strategy-cicd-litmus/understanding-cicd.html).

question.en: Why do mature pipelines build one artifact and promote it through environments instead of rebuilding per environment, and what breaks if you rebuild?

answer.en: The artifact that passed the tests must be the artifact that ships. A rebuild is not guaranteed to be identical: dependency resolution can drift when versions are not pinned, build metadata differs, and the fresh build can even fail or pick up changed source. Rebuilding per environment means the bits verified in staging are not provably the bits running in production, which destroys the audit chain from test to release (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/strategy-cicd-litmus/understanding-cicd.html).

question.en: What is the difference between a Docker image and a container, and why use a multi-stage build?

answer.en:
An image is the packaged template built from Dockerfile instructions; a container is a running instance created from that image. Docker images are built in layers, so instruction order and build context affect caching. A multi-stage Dockerfile separates compilation or dependency installation from the runtime stage. The final stage copies only the required artifact, leaving build tools and intermediate files out of the production image. That usually reduces image size and attack surface, while keeping the build definition in one file. I would also use a suitable minimal base, avoid embedding secrets, and run the application as a non-root user where the runtime permits it.

```dockerfile caption="Build dependencies stay in the build stage; the runtime stage copies the output."
FROM node:22-alpine AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

FROM node:22-alpine AS runtime
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]
```

question.en: In a multi-stage build, do the earlier stages' layers end up in the final image, and what exactly does `COPY --from=build` transfer?

answer.en: No. Each FROM starts an independent stage and only the last stage becomes the image; earlier stages exist only while building. `COPY --from=build` copies files out of that stage's filesystem into the final stage as an ordinary new layer; it does not import or reference the build stage's layers (https://docs.docker.com/build/building/multi-stage/).

question.en: Why does the reviewed Dockerfile copy package*.json and run npm ci before copying the source, and what happens to build time if you copy everything first?

answer.en: Docker caches layers in order and invalidates everything from the first instruction whose inputs changed. With the manifests copied first, the npm ci layer is reused as long as the package files do not change, so a source-only edit skips dependency installation entirely. If `COPY . .` comes first, every source edit also invalidates the install layer and npm ci reruns on each build (https://docs.docker.com/build/concepts/dockerfile/).

question.en: How should a pipeline manage environment-specific configuration and secrets?

answer.en:
I keep deployable artifacts environment-neutral and inject environment-specific configuration at deployment or runtime. Non-sensitive settings can be versioned as reviewed configuration; credentials and tokens belong in a managed secret store or CI secret facility, never in the repository or image. Access should be scoped to the job and environment that needs it, and production promotion should have an explicit gate where appropriate. In GitHub Actions, an environment can restrict branches, require reviewers, and limit access to environment secrets; those secrets become available only to jobs that reference the environment and pass its protection rules. I also design rotation, auditability, and safe logging from the start.

```yaml caption="An environment-scoped job can consume a protected secret without committing it."
jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production
    steps:
      - run: ./deploy
        env:
          API_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.API_TOKEN }}
```

question.en: A job uses `${{ secrets.PROD_KEY }}`, but PROD_KEY is stored in the protected production environment and the job does not declare that environment. What does the job get?

answer.en: The secret is simply not available: environment secrets are exposed only to jobs that reference the environment and pass its protection rules, such as required reviewers and branch restrictions (https://docs.github.com/en/actions/concepts/deployment-environments). There is no parse-time error and no automatic fallback; the value is not injected, so the failure surfaces later, typically as an authentication error against the deploy target. Declaring `environment: production` on the job is what brings both the gate and the secret into scope.

question.en: A debug step printed a secret into a job log and GitHub redacted it. Is the leak contained?

answer.en: No. GitHub automatically redacts secret values printed to workflow logs, but the documentation is clear that because a value can be transformed in multiple ways, for example substrings or encodings, the redaction is not guaranteed (https://docs.github.com/en/actions/concepts/security/secrets). Anyone with access to the log may also hold surrounding context. The correct response is to remove the logging step, treat the secret as exposed, and rotate it.

question.en: How would you serve a static frontend from S3 through CloudFront securely?

answer.en: I would store the built assets in an S3 bucket and use CloudFront with that bucket as the origin. I would keep the bucket private and grant the distribution access through CloudFront Origin Access Control, with an S3 bucket policy constrained to the distribution. AWS recommends OAC over the older Origin Access Identity for current scenarios, including broader Region support and SSE-KMS compatibility. The deployment should upload immutable or versioned assets, invalidate only what needs invalidation, and configure the correct cache behavior and error handling for the application. DNS and TLS are part of the edge configuration, but they do not replace origin authorization.

question.en: With a private bucket and Origin Access Control, what happens when a user requests the object's s3.amazonaws.com URL directly, bypassing CloudFront?

answer.en: S3 returns Access Denied. The bucket policy grants s3:GetObject only to the cloudfront.amazonaws.com service principal, with an AWS:SourceArn condition pinning the grant to that specific distribution, so every other principal, including an anonymous browser request to the S3 endpoint, is refused (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/private-content-restricting-access-to-s3.html). That is the design goal: the bucket is unreadable except through the distribution, so TLS, caching, and edge-level restrictions cannot be bypassed.

question.en: Your build hashes asset filenames, but index.html keeps the same key on every deploy. What should the pipeline invalidate, and what is the cost of invalidating /* each time?

answer.en: Hashed assets are immutable: a new build produces new keys and the old keys can stay cached. Only the HTML entry point, and anything else stored under a stable key, needs invalidation, so the pipeline should invalidate that path or give it a short TTL or a versioned key. Invalidating /* works but flushes every object at every edge location, which is slower, consumes invalidation capacity, and throws away warm cache for content that did not change (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/private-content-restricting-access-to-s3.html).

question.en: What permissions and deployment steps are needed when API Gateway invokes Lambda?

answer.en: There are two different permission paths to reason about. The API caller needs permission to invoke the deployed API when IAM authorization is used. Separately, API Gateway needs permission to invoke the Lambda integration, commonly through a Lambda resource policy or an appropriate service role depending on the integration. Lambda itself needs an execution role granting only the AWS actions it requires, such as writing logs or accessing a named data resource. After defining the method and integration, the API must be deployed to a stage; changes to the API do not affect a stage until redeployed. I would test the complete deployed path, not only a console simulation.

question.en: You added a method in the API Gateway console, but the stage URL still behaves like the old API. Why?

answer.en: A stage points at a deployment, which is a snapshot of the API at the moment it was deployed. Console edits change the API's definition but do not touch the stage until you create a new deployment to it. The same applies to infrastructure-as-code changes: the tool updates the API definition, and the stage only moves when a deployment is created or updated (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/services-apigateway-tutorial.html).

question.en: A caller gets a 403 on an IAM-authorized method. Which of the two permission paths do you investigate first?

answer.en: The two paths fail differently. With IAM authorization, the caller's identity needs execute-api:Invoke on the API's execution ARN, and an explicit deny anywhere wins; a failure on this path is the 403. Separately, API Gateway needs permission to invoke the Lambda integration, granted through the function's resource policy or an appropriate service role; a failure on that path typically surfaces as a server error from the integration, not as the caller's 403. Separating the paths avoids the classic wrong fix of granting the caller lambda:InvokeFunction (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/apigateway/latest/developerguide/permissions.html).

question.en: How do you apply least privilege to CI/CD and AWS workloads?

answer.en: I model each actor separately: the CI identity, deployment role, runtime role, and human operators should not share one broad credential. Policies should allow only the required actions, resources, and conditions, using resource ARNs rather than wildcards where practical. A role trust policy answers who may assume a role; its permissions policies answer what the role may do. I prefer short-lived or federated credentials for automation, separate accounts or environments where the risk warrants it, and protected production approvals. Finally, I review access with logs and tests, remove unused permissions, and ensure the pipeline cannot print secrets. Least privilege is an operating process, not a one-time JSON exercise.

question.en: A role's trust policy names your CI system as a trusted principal. Does that trust policy define what the pipeline can do in your account?

answer.en: No. The trust policy answers only who may assume the role; what the assumed role may do is defined by its permission policies. The pipeline's effective power is the combination: it must be allowed to assume the role, and then everything it does is capped by the role's permissions. Reviewing only one of the two documents always gives a false picture of access (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/security-iam.html).

question.en: You tightened a deployment role and the next deploy failed at runtime, even though the change plan reviewed cleanly. Why does static review of the policy JSON miss this, and what catches it?

answer.en: IAM evaluates each request when it happens. A policy that omits an action only fails when a code path actually makes that call, and nothing in the JSON reveals which calls the deploy will make. What catches it is exercising the real flows: running the deployment in a lower environment, reading the deny from the error output or logs, and iterating until observed access matches the policy. That is why least privilege is an operating process of review and removal, not a one-time JSON exercise (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/apigateway/latest/developerguide/security-iam.html).

question.en: Explain the basic Terraform workflow and why state matters in CI.

answer.en:
The basic workflow is write configuration, initialize providers and modules, plan the proposed changes, review the plan, and apply it. `terraform plan` compares configuration and recorded state with the real provider objects but does not change infrastructure; `terraform apply` executes a plan. State maps declared resource instances to real objects, so it is essential for deciding what to create, update, or destroy. In a team, I use a remote backend with locking and controlled access rather than an unmanaged local state file. In automation, I generate a reviewed plan artifact and apply that exact plan, while handling failed applies explicitly because Terraform does not automatically roll back partial changes.

```bash caption="A reviewed saved plan makes the automated apply correspond to the reviewed change."
terraform init
terraform plan -out=plan.tfplan
# review plan.tfplan in CI
terraform apply plan.tfplan
```

question.en: `terraform apply` fails halfway through creating resources. What does the infrastructure look like now, and what does Terraform do about it?

answer.en: Terraform does not roll back. The resources created before the failure exist and are recorded in state, which is written incrementally as the apply progresses, so the partial state is accurate. The correct response is to read the error, fix the cause, and apply again: the next plan sees the partially created set and proposes only the remaining changes. Assuming apply is transactional is the dangerous mistake, because it leads to orphaned, billed resources that nobody cleans up (https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/state).

question.en: CI generated and reviewed tfplan on the pull request. Another change merged to main before the apply job ran `terraform apply tfplan`. What gets applied?

answer.en: The saved plan is what gets applied: applying a plan file executes the changes captured when the plan was generated, not a fresh plan of the current configuration (https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cli/commands/apply). That is the mechanism that makes the reviewed change the applied change, and it is also the trap: if the configuration moved on, the applied plan no longer matches the repository, and the next run will show a diff. This is why the core workflow tells teams to review the final concrete plan after merge, since merge order and recent changes can alter it (https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/intro/core-workflow). Robust pipelines generate the plan from the exact commit being promoted, or re-plan after merge and review that final plan.

question.en: How do feature flags complement continuous delivery, and what operational risks do they introduce?

answer.en: A feature flag decouples deploying code from exposing behavior: code can reach production while a flag keeps a capability off or limits it to selected contexts. That supports trunk-based integration and progressive release, but it adds runtime decision paths and configuration dependency. I define an owner, purpose, default-safe behavior, exposure metrics, expiration date, and rollback procedure for every temporary flag. Rollouts should be observable and reversible, and the old path should be removed when the flag is no longer needed. Progressive rollouts allocate a specified percentage of contexts and increase it over time; they are not a substitute for tests, compatibility checks, or a rollback plan.

question.en: A flag has been fully on for three months. What does it cost to leave it on, and what does removing it actually involve?

answer.en: Leaving it on accrues flag debt: every flag adds a runtime decision path, extra test combinations, and a configuration dependency that can fail independently of the code. Removing a temporary flag is a code change: delete the dead path and the flag wiring, adjust the tests, and ship it, which itself needs review, deployment, and a rollback plan. That is why every temporary flag should be created with an owner and an expiration date, so cleanup is scheduled work instead of archaeology (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/strategy-cicd-litmus/understanding-cicd.html).

question.en: The flag evaluation service is unavailable at request time and the flag's configured default is off. What should the application do?

answer.en: Fail safe to the default: serve the known-good path with the flag off, degrade gracefully, and surface the evaluation failure in metrics instead of failing the request. This is why the default state must be chosen for safety rather than novelty: the default is what runs during outages, bad configurations, and first deployments. Failing open, meaning treating the outage as 'on', couples your release exposure to the flag service's uptime (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/strategy-cicd-litmus/understanding-cicd.html).

question.en: When would you choose all-at-once, blue/green, canary, or linear deployment?

answer.en: All-at-once is simplest and fastest, but it exposes the whole traffic population immediately. Blue/green runs a replacement environment so it can be verified before traffic is switched, at the cost of extra capacity and coordination. Canary sends an initial fraction of traffic and then the remainder after an observation interval; linear shifts traffic in equal increments. I choose based on blast radius, startup time, state and schema compatibility, traffic control, monitoring quality, and rollback speed. The strategy is incomplete without automated health checks, a bake or observation period where appropriate, and a tested way to return traffic to the known-good version.

question.en: Blue/green promises rollback by switching traffic back to blue. When is that promise false?

answer.en: The traffic switch is only a rollback if blue is still intact and both versions are compatible at the data layer. If green ran a backward-incompatible schema migration or wrote records blue cannot read, routing traffic back does not undo the data: blue now fails on the same records. This is why the choice hinges on state and schema compatibility, and why green must be verified with real traffic shapes before the switch, with a tested way to return traffic to the known-good version (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECS/latest/developerguide/deployment-type-bluegreen.html).

question.en: A canary at 10% ran for 10 minutes with no alarms, so it was promoted to full traffic. On a low-traffic service, why might that prove nothing?

answer.en: Alarms need enough requests to be statistically meaningful. Ten percent of a low-traffic service for ten minutes can be a handful of requests, far below any error-rate threshold, so a badly broken build can pass a 'clean' canary. The canary percentage and bake time must be chosen against real traffic volume and monitoring quality, and a canary only measures what is actually instrumented; on low traffic you need longer bake times or synthetic traffic before shifting (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codedeploy/latest/userguide/deployment-configurations.html).
